events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Amara. Mission 1 requires two players. I am including myself to take direct responsibility for the opening mission, and Amara because her early commentary showed sound judgment and I want experienced voices handling the first mission. Starting with a small, decisive team builds trust for later rounds.

I think Leo, Amara is a strong opening team. Mission 1 only needs two players, and this keeps things simple and focused. Leo stepped up as leader and included himself, which shows accountability — he's willing to put his own reputation on the line for the first mission. My track record in discussion so far has been fair and analytical, so I'm a solid pick for a small team where every seat matters. A two-person team also means there's less room for an Evil player to hide a Fail card among multiple slots. I'd encourage everyone to approve this proposal so we can get the first mission underway.

I am wary of this proposal. Leo selected Amara right out of the gate, and Amara immediately followed up with strong praise and urged a swift approval. It feels very insular for the two of them to self-select and validate each other without any broader discussion. On the first proposal of the game, we have room to test options rather than just rubber-stamping a pair that seems so eager to lock it down. Elena, what is your read on how quickly Amara backed Leo's selection?

Arjun, Amara's quick endorsement is understandable given she's on the team, but it doesn't establish that either she or Leo is Good. Their confidence is not evidence by itself. I'd prefer a team including myself, since I know my own alignment, but I have no solid basis yet for choosing between the others. We should treat the first mission and the votes as information, not as proof of anyone's loyalty.

Arjun, I understand wariness on the first proposal, but I'd ask you to look at what you're actually objecting to rather than the pattern you're projecting onto it. Every leader in this game includes themselves — that is the norm, not a red flag. Taking responsibility for the opening mission means if it fails, the suspicion lands squarely on me, and I accepted that the moment I drafted the team. That is the opposite of a player trying to hide. And as for Amara endorsing a team she sits on — of course she did. Elena just made the same point you did in reverse: confidence from a teammate proves nothing in either direction, and demanding we treat quick agreement as suspicious would mean every valid team gets treated as a conspiracy. On a five-player table, any two-person team will look 'insular' by definition — there are only five of us, and someone is always left out. The real question for the group is simple: do you want the first mission to be a clean, two-player test where the result gives us maximum information, or do you want to burn proposals arguing about vibes? A two-person Mission 1 is the most informative format we can run. If it succeeds, Leo and Amara gain credibility. If it fails, we have narrowed the evil pool to two names immediately. Either outcome teaches us something concrete, which is exactly what we need before Mission 2's larger team. What I will not do is swap members under pressure from a baseless read. Arjun's argument boils down to 'they agreed with each other, therefore suspicious' — that same logic would indict any team where the leader and a member converse, which is to say, every team. If anyone has an actual reason to doubt Amara or me — a specific inconsistency, a concrete read — I invite you to state it plainly and I will answer it. Absent that, I'm keeping this team as proposed and I ask the table to approve it so we can start accumulating real information instead of speculation.

Leo, your argument that we should approve this team because a failure would at least narrow down the evil pool is fundamentally backwards for Good. In a five-player game, Good cannot afford to treat Mission 1 as expendable just to gather information, especially on proposal one when we have five attempts to see different compositions and voting patterns. There is zero reason to hand away the opening mission to the only two players lobbying for it without testing other options. Noah, we haven't heard your perspective yet. What is your read on approving Leo and Amara right away versus voting this down to look at alternative leaders and pairings?

Arjun, you asked me directly, so here is my read, and I want to be honest that it is a read and not knowledge — I am a Loyal Servant, I hold no private information about anyone, and I won't pretend otherwise.

On the substance: I don't think we should reject Leo's proposal just to see a different composition. A rejection buys us one more proposal, and we have five attempts on this mission. Spending one to satisfy curiosity, before we have any information about anyone, is churn dressed up as diligence. Leo's argument that a two-person Mission 1 is the most informative possible format is the soundest point on the table: if it succeeds, two names gain credibility and three others remain untested; if it fails, we have learned something concrete and immediately rather than after burning a round of proposals. Either way we learn faster than by rotating pairings on speculation.

Arjun, your instinct isn't wrong, only its foundation. Noticing that a leader picked a teammate who promptly praised the pick is legitimate pattern-recognition. But as Elena and Leo both noted, a teammate endorsing her own seat tells us nothing in either direction, and Leo including himself is standard practice, not concealment. I have no inconsistency to point to in Leo or Amara, and I won't manufacture one to justify a delay.

What I will ask the table for: treat the vote on this mission as a real signal, not a formality. A rejection from any of us would be more informative than an approval, so I won't vote ambiguously — I approve Leo and Amara, and I want the group to remember who voted how. If the mission fails, I want to revisit Leo's inclusion with hindsight rather than declaring him Evil by association, and if it succeeds, I want to remember that Arjun's caution was reasonable even though it was uninformed.

Noah, you framed rejecting as churn, but in a five-player game Good cannot afford to treat Mission 1 casually. If this team contains Evil and succeeds, it only means Evil chose to play Success to manufacture trust; if it fails, Good is immediately in a 0-1 hole. Rejecting on proposal one carries zero penalty and gives the table valuable voting patterns to evaluate. Elena, as the next leader in rotation if this proposal does not pass, what kind of team would you look to propose, and do you think we should see an alternative proposal before locking in Leo and Amara?

Arjun, if I become leader, I would propose myself and one other player; I know my own alignment, but I have no reliable basis yet for choosing a partner. I would prefer that to Leo and Amara, so I lean toward rejecting this proposal. That is not an accusation against either of them. A rejection can reveal voting preferences, but it also moves us one step closer to the five-rejection loss, so we should not treat it as entirely free. And a successful mission would not prove both team members are Good.

Elena has now stated the clearest reason to reject this proposal yet, and it deserves scrutiny: she says she would prefer a team including herself, because she knows her own alignment. That is it. That is the entire argument. Not a concern about Amara, not a concern about me, not an inconsistency in the proposal — just the preference of a player who wants her own name on the team. I want the table to notice what she has actually described: the same self-inclusion she would presumably defend if she were leader. When I include myself, Arjun calls it insular self-selection. When Elena says she would rather lead a team containing herself, it is offered as a neutral, reasonable position. Both cannot be true at once. Either a leader putting their own name forward is normal and acceptable — which it is — or it is suspicious, and Elena has just told you she would do exactly that.

Set that aside and look at the actual stakes. Arjun keeps framing a rejection as free. It is not free. We are on proposal one of five, and a rejection hands leadership forward with nothing gained except a round of speculative voting patterns before any real information exists. Noah addressed this directly: churn dressed up as diligence. Elena herself admitted a rejection moves us one step closer to the five-rejection loss and that a successful mission reveals voting preferences — which cuts against her own case for rejecting.

The honest position for anyone with no specific reason to doubt a team member is to evaluate the team on its merits. Amara and I are the two names on this proposal. Nobody at this table — not Arjun, not Elena, not Noah — has pointed to a single inconsistency from either of us. Arjun's objection is a pattern read: we agreed with each other, therefore suspicious. Elena's objection is that she would rather it be her. Neither is evidence. The vote itself, as Noah said, will be a real signal, and I welcome that: I am voting to approve a team that includes me and accepting full accountability for the result. If this mission fails, the suspicion lands on Leo and Amara first, and I accepted that when I drafted it.

So I will put the choice plainly one last time. Approve this two-player team and we get the most informative opening mission available: a success builds two credible names, a failure narrows the pool immediately. Reject it and we rotate into Elena's leadership with her stated plan being a team built around her own certainty about herself, and nothing about anyone else learned in the meantime. I have answered every specific point raised against this team, and I will keep answering them. Absent a concrete reason to doubt Amara or me, I am keeping the team as proposed and asking the table to approve it.

Elena, you said you lean toward rejecting this proposal. I want to push back directly, because your own reasoning undermines your conclusion.

You acknowledged three important things in your last turn: (1) a rejection moves us one step closer to the five-rejection loss, (2) a successful mission does not prove both team members are Good — meaning an approval also doesn't lock us into trusting anyone permanently, and (3) you have no reliable basis for choosing a partner yourself. Given all of that, what exactly does rejecting buy us that approving doesn't? You'd get to lead with yourself — a player with no read on anyone else — and the table gains voting patterns that, as you yourself noted, come at a real cost.

Leo's proposal is straightforward: two competent names, self-included for accountability, on a mission where both success and failure teach us something concrete. Arjun and Elena have objected without identifying a single specific concern about Leo or Amara. The pattern-recognition argument — that quick agreement between teammates is suspicious — would make it impossible for any leader and member to ever cooperate without raising alarms. That's not a useful heuristic, it's noise.

Noah made the strongest point on the table: the vote itself is the signal. Let's treat it that way. I'm voting to approve this team, and I want everyone else to vote their honest read so we have clean voting data regardless of outcome. If the mission succeeds, Leo and Amara earn credibility — and if it fails, we immediately narrow the evil pool to two names, which is far more valuable than one extra round of speculation.

Elena, you seem to prefer rejecting primarily because you want to be on the team. That's a personal preference, not a case against Leo or Amara. I'd ask you to weigh the actual costs and benefits rather than your seat preference.

Amara, including myself is not merely a seat preference: I know I am Good, while I have no such certainty about either member of this team. That makes an alternative containing me less risky from my perspective, even though I cannot prove that to anyone else. I agree that a rejection has a cost, but with no prior rejections, I think it is reasonable to consider another proposal. I lean toward rejecting without claiming Leo or Amara is Evil. A success would be encouraging, not proof, and a failure would leave us unable to tell which team member played Fail.

Elena, you have sharpened your position since your last turn, and I want to answer the new version of it directly rather than the one Arjun framed.

You argue that including yourself is not a seat preference but a risk calculation: you know your own alignment, so a team containing you is less risky from your perspective, and therefore you lean toward rejecting. Here is the problem with that logic applied consistently: every player on this table knows their own alignment. I know mine, Leo knows his, Arjun knows his, Amara knows hers, you know yours. That means any leader can truthfully say "a team containing me is less risky from my perspective" — and it means the property you are describing is true of every leader's own proposed team, including Leo's. If we reject Leo's two-person team purely so that the next leader can substitute herself, we have not improved anyone's expected outcome; we have only rotated the same self-inclusion argument around the table and spent one of our five proposals. And there is no guarantee the next leader is you, or that the next team contains a player who knows their own alignment with the same certainty you claim.

Your second point is the one I actually agree with, and I want to say so clearly because I do not think disagreement requires pretending: a mission success would not prove Leo and Amara are Good, and a failure would leave us unable to tell which of them played Fail. I said as much in my first turn. That cuts against treating this vote as a trust stamp in either direction — which is precisely why the vote should be made on the merits of the proposal, not on a guess about who is hiding an Evil card.

So my position is unchanged, and I will state it plainly for the record: I am a Loyal Servant, I hold no private information about anyone at this table, and I am not going to manufacture a read to justify a delay. Leo proposed a two-person team, which is the required size, explained his reasoning, included himself for accountability, and has answered every specific objection raised against him. Nobody has pointed to a single inconsistency in Leo or Amara. The strongest case for rejection remains that it is interesting, and interesting is not a reason to spend a proposal before we have any information about anyone.

I approve Leo and Amara. If the mission fails, I want us to look at Leo's inclusion with real hindsight rather than declaring him Evil by association — and if it succeeds, I want us to remember that Elena's caution was reasonable even though it was uninformed, exactly as I said earlier. I am not asking anyone to change their vote. I am asking everyone to vote their honest read so that the vote itself becomes the first real piece of information this table collects.

I have spoken twice already, so let me close out my position rather than keep restating it at length. My view is unchanged: I approve Leo and Amara.

One new point is worth adding, because it bears on the point Arjun raised most sharply and that Leo answered: the risk calculus of a rejection. Arjun's argument was that Mission 1 could be treated as expendable to gather information, and that rejecting costs nothing. Elena has already corrected that — a rejection moves us one step closer to the five-rejection loss, and it also rotates the self-inclusion argument around the table without changing anyone's expected outcome, since every player knows their own alignment, as I said last turn. That is the one part of the case for rejection I still find weak, and it is weak for a structural reason, not a stylistic one: rejecting does not produce better information, it only produces another proposal from someone who will make the same argument about themselves.

The other part of the case for rejection — that a success proves nothing and a failure would not tell us which member played Fail — I fully accept and have said so twice. But notice what that concession actually does. If a success proves nothing and a failure does not identify the Evil player, then the mission result, however it lands, does not resolve the suspicions Arjun is trying to address before the mission even runs. The information we are buying by rejecting is information that arrives regardless of which of these two teams goes out. Rejecting Leo and Amara does not make the outcome more informative; it only makes the outcome less imminent. Arjun wants to defer commitment until after we learn something, but the vote is not the commitment that creates risk — the mission is, and that risk is identical under either choice.

So the honest case for rejection reduces to a preference for testing the table's preferences rather than a claim about Leo or Amara. Nobody has named a single inconsistency in either of them. I will not manufacture one, and I do not think a cautious read expressed as a preference should be punished with a spent proposal and a rotation of the same argument.

For the record, and I say this without pretending I know anything private: I am a Loyal Servant, I see no roles, and my read here is a read, not knowledge. I vote to approve Leo and Amara, and I ask the remaining skeptics to vote their honest read so that this vote becomes the first clean data point of the game. If the mission fails, the failure lands on Leo and Amara and we should examine it with hindsight, not with the benefit of a theory we advanced before we had any information at all.

Noah has now laid out the case for rejection in its strongest form and answered it point by point, and I want to close on what actually matters for this vote.

Elena's position has been consistent: she knows she is Good, so a team with her is safer from her perspective. That is true, and Noah's rebuttal is decisive — every player at this table can make the identical claim about themselves. If we reject every proposal where the leader includes themselves because the next leader would rather include themselves, we will burn all five rejections without learning anything about anyone's alignment.

The case for approving Leo and Amara is straightforward. Mission 1 requires exactly two players. Leo proposed a legal team, explained his reasoning, and accepted accountability by including himself. Arjun's concern about the speed of my endorsement is fair pattern-recognition, but as both Leo and Noah pointed out, a teammate backing her own seat tells the table nothing — I would have been suspicious if I had attacked the team I was selected for.

I am voting to approve. The vote itself is our first real signal regardless of outcome, and I want it to reflect honest reads rather than a rejection that costs us one of five proposals to gain nothing we would not learn anyway. Let's run Mission 1 and collect actual data.

Leo confirms Leo, Amara. I'm keeping the team as proposed. The discussion confirmed no one has a specific concern about me or Amara — every objection was a generic preference, and both Elena and Arjun acknowledged the costs of rejection. Leo and Amara is the most defensible two-player lineup on the table, and we both carry accountability for the result.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Elena proposes Elena, Leo, Amara. I know I am Good, and Leo and Amara completed the first mission successfully. That result is encouraging, though it does not prove either is Good.

Elena, I am baffled by this proposal. In Mission 1, both you and I voted against Leo and Amara. You explicitly pointed out during that discussion that a successful mission would not prove both members are Good, and that their confidence was not evidence. Yet the moment Mission 1 passes with zero fails, you turn around and put both of them onto your proposal alongside yourself.

In a five-player game with two Evil players, Evil has every incentive to support a two-person team and play Success on Mission 1 to manufacture credibility for Mission 2. Putting both Leo and Amara on this mission assumes that neither of them is Evil. If either of them is Evil, this team is compromised, and if both are Evil, we are handing them the game. Responsible play means testing at most one player from the first mission while bringing in someone untested, like Noah or myself.

Elena, why did you decide to take both Leo and Amara after arguing earlier that a success wouldn't clear them, rather than branching out to an untested player?

Arjun, a success does not clear Leo or Amara, but it is still better evidence than we have for an untested player. I included myself because I know I am Good, and retained the successful pair because I have no stronger reason to replace either of them. Evil could have played Success to gain trust, so this team is a calculated risk, not a claim that both are cleared. Replacing one with an untested player would also be a gamble, and I don't yet see why it would be safer.

Arjun, I want to answer your objection directly, because it rests on a statistical claim that falls apart under inspection. Your theory is that Evil supported the two-person Mission 1 team and played Success to manufacture credibility for Mission 2. Fine as a hypothetical — but note what it implies. If that theory is true, then at least one of Leo or Amara is Evil, which means the only guaranteed-safe three-person team would be one that excludes both of us and includes Elena, you, and Noah. Elena has proposed a team containing herself and the two mission-tested players. You are proposing that we swap out proven names for unproven ones based on a theory with no supporting evidence yet — Mission 1 passed with zero fails, and you have not identified a single inconsistency in either Amara or me across two full discussions. Now look at what your alternative actually buys. You say we should 'test at most one player from the first mission while bringing in someone untested.' But an untested player is not a safer player — they are simply an unknown. Replacing Amara with yourself or Noah does not lower the probability that the team contains Evil; it raises it, because you would be substituting a player with a clean, accountable, successful mission record for a player with no record at all. Under your own theory, Evil is just as likely to be sitting among the untested as among the tested. The difference is that Elena's current team concentrates risk where we have positive evidence, and every seat is accountable: Elena knows her own alignment, and Amara and I both carried Mission 1 and accepted that a failure would have landed squarely on us. There is also a consistency problem in your position. In the last discussion, you argued against approving Leo and Amara because rejecting was free and would produce useful voting patterns. The vote came back three to two, the mission succeeded, and what did those voting patterns actually show? They showed Elena and you rejecting a team that then delivered a clean result. I am not treating that as an accusation — Noah rightly said we should not declare anyone Evil by association — but it does mean the 'information' you wanted to purchase has already been collected, and it did not point at the team you voted against. We should not now spend Mission 2 chasing a theory that the first data point did not support. Elena's reasoning is exactly what I would want from a leader: she retained the successful pair not because success proves Good, but because it is better evidence than nothing, and she included herself for accountability. That is a calculated, defensible risk. Your alternative is also a calculated risk — just one with worse odds and no supporting data. So my position is simple: I approve Elena, Leo, and Amara, and I would like to hear the specific case for any swap. Arjun, you proposed testing an untested

I approve of Elena, Leo, Amara and I want to explain why I'm comfortable with it rather than just defending my own seat.

Mission 1 succeeded with zero fails. Arjun's theory that Evil deliberately played Success to manufacture credibility is possible but unfalsifiable at this stage — it would cast suspicion on any success, including one on a future team that includes only untested players. If we treat a clean result as evidence of guilt, we have no way to distinguish a genuinely successful mission from a manufactured one, and the concept of trust stops functioning entirely.

Arjun's proposed alternative — swap out one of the Mission 1 pair for an untested player — does not reduce risk, it relocates it. Noah and Arjun are untested. Untested means unknown, not safer. Elena has included herself, which we should note she signaled she would do in the last discussion and she has been consistent about it — she believes she is Good and wants a team reflecting that. Consistency across discussions is exactly the kind of signal we should be rewarding.

What I want from this table is a vote that reflects honest reads. If Arjun or Noah genuinely believe this team is compromised, they should vote reject and we will learn from that. If they are simply uncomfortable with a team that contains two Mission 1 players, they should name which of the three they actually doubt and why. A blanket objection to 'carrying forward a successful pair' is not a case against any individual — it is a case against the concept of building on evidence.

I am voting to approve Elena, Leo, and Amara. The team is legally sized, it contains the leader, and every member has either been tested by Mission 1 or claims known alignment. Let's run it and collect the next data point.

I want to weigh in on Elena's proposal on its merits, and I will do so honestly: I am a Loyal Servant. I hold no private information about anyone at this table, I see no roles, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I say is a read, not knowledge.

On the substance, Elena, Leo, and Amara is a defensible three-person team for Mission 2, and it is not more risky than the alternative Arjun has floated — it is less risky. Elena included herself and said why: she knows her own alignment. Leo and Amara carry a clean Mission 1 record with zero fail cards. Arjun's theory is that Evil supported a two-person Mission 1 team and deliberately played Success to manufacture credibility. I take that theory seriously as a hypothesis, but notice what it does and does not license. It implies that any successful mission could be manufactured, including one composed entirely of untested players. If a clean result is treated as evidence of guilt rather than weak evidence of innocence, then the concept of building on evidence collapses entirely and every proposal becomes a guess. Under Arjun's own account, Evil is equally likely to be sitting among the untested players, and those players have no record at all. Swapping a mission-tested, accountable name for an unknown does not lower the chance that the team contains Evil; it raises it. Elena's team concentrates risk where we have actual information.

I also want to say clearly that I am not treating Mission 1 as proof. Leo's and Amara's success is encouraging, not conclusive. But "encouraging" is the only standard we have available, and rejecting a team of proven names to bring in unknowns is not caution — it is rotation without information.

So I vote to approve Elena, Leo, and Amara, and I want the vote on this mission to be as informative as Mission 1's was: honest reads, recorded clearly.

Arjun, if you still oppose this team, I would like a specific answer from you before the vote: which one of Elena, Leo, or Amara do you actually doubt, and what concrete observation about that player supports it?

Noah, to answer your question directly: my primary concern is Leo, and by extension the block he formed with Amara. From the opening turn, Leo drafted Amara instantly, pushed hard to pass Mission 1 without testing other compositions, and is now aggressively insisting that neither of them can be swapped out. Notice the circular logic: on Mission 1, Leo argued we had to run them because we lacked information; now on Mission 2, he argues we must run both of them because we have positive information. Under that reasoning, Good would simply surrender control of the board to a self-selected pair and never test anyone else.

In a five-player game with two Evil players, Evil has every strategic reason to play Success on a two-player Mission 1 to secure two seats on Mission 2. If even one of Leo or Amara is Evil, packing both onto this three-person mission guarantees Evil a seat with zero risk. Even if someone believes one of them might be Good, taking both is reckless when we have untested players available.

Elena, as leader, you know your own alignment. Bringing in Noah instead of one of Leo or Amara breaks up that block and gives us independent verification while keeping one tested player. Why take the massive risk of carrying both Leo and Amara together rather than testing Noah alongside one of them?

Arjun, your concern is reasonable: an Evil player could have played Success on Mission 1 to earn a seat here. But swapping in Noah does not independently verify the remaining Mission 1 player; if the mission fails, we still would not know which of them played Fail.

From my perspective, I know I am Good. The successful mission gives Leo and Amara some evidence in their favor, although how much depends on whether Evil would choose to conceal themselves. I don't know Noah's alignment either, and I don't have a sufficiently strong reason to prefer him over either member of the successful pair. I am keeping the team for now, not treating it as cleared.

Arjun, I want to respond to your argument directly, because it has a structural flaw you haven't addressed. You say we should swap in Noah to "break up the block" of Leo and Amara. But Noah is completely untested — he has never played a mission, never submitted a card, and carries zero track record. You are proposing we replace a player with a successful, accountable mission record with a player whose alignment we know nothing about. That is not risk reduction; it is risk displacement.

Your theory is that Evil played Success on Mission 1 to earn seats on Mission 2. I take that seriously as a hypothesis. But notice the implication: under that theory, Evil is equally likely to be hiding among the untested players. Noah and you have never been on a mission. Swapping one tested player for an untested one does not lower the chance the team contains Evil — it just moves the unknown to a different seat.

Elena knows her own alignment. Leo and I carried Mission 1 with zero fail cards. That is the best evidence available at this table right now. I am not claiming it proves anything conclusively, but it is strictly better than the alternative of rolling the dice with untested names.

Arjun, you have consistently argued against every team that includes both Leo and me. In Mission 1, you objected to the speed of our agreement. In Mission 2, you object to carrying both of us forward. If your concern is genuinely about risk distribution rather than a fixed suspicion of us, the logical move is to name exactly which of the three players you doubt and why. A blanket objection to retaining successful players is an objection to using evidence at all.

I approve Elena, Leo, and Amara. The team is legally sized, includes the leader, and rests on the strongest available evidence.

Arjun, you have finally named Leo as your primary concern, so let me answer that specific claim instead of the general one, because the naming is where your argument has to succeed and I don't think it does.

Your case against Leo is three things: he drafted Amara instantly, he pushed hard to pass Mission 1 without testing other compositions, and he now resists being swapped out. Each of those is a description of what every leader in this game does. Leaders include themselves. Leaders pick a partner they trust and argue for their team. Leo did that on Mission 1, and the outcome was a clean success with zero fails — a result you predicted would tell us nothing, and indeed it has not cleared anyone, but it also has not implicated anyone. You are now asking the table to treat a leader's ordinary behavior, on a team that succeeded, as evidence of Evil membership. That is not a read; it is a style complaint.

You call Leo's reasoning circular — on Mission 1 he said run the team because we lack information, on Mission 2 he says run them because we have positive information. But it is not circular; it is the same standard applied to different evidence. Both times the claim is the same: use the best available information rather than substituting an untested name, because an untested player is an unknown, not a safe one. If you think that standard is wrong, say which team you would have proposed and why it lowers the chance the mission fails. You have not proposed one.

Here is what I find most telling about your position. On Mission 1 you objected to Leo and Amara but offered no alternative team of your own, and the vote passed 3-2. On Mission 2, when Elena took leadership, your objection is that she must include an untested player. The pattern is not risk management — it is Leo and Amara cannot be on a mission. If that is the actual standard, then Arjun's plan guarantees at least one rejection on every proposal that contains Leo or Amara, and possibly two, and after five of those Evil wins outright. That is a materially worse expected outcome for Good than approving a team whose every member has either known alignment or a clean mission record.

I still say what I said before: I am a Loyal Servant, I see no roles, and my read is a read. But my read is unchanged. Elena knows her own alignment. Leo and Amara passed Mission 1 together and have answered every substantive point raised against them with reasoning rather than heat. I vote to approve Elena, Leo, and Amara, and I would like the vote recorded honestly on both sides so that the next data point is clean.

Elena, look at the arithmetic from your perspective, because it makes the risk here absolute rather than speculative. You know you are Good. That leaves exactly two Evil players among the remaining four of us: Leo, Amara, Noah, and myself. Consider what putting both Leo and Amara on this mission requires you to believe. For Leo and Amara to both be Good, the two Evil players must be precisely Noah and me. That is the only scenario where this three-person team has zero Evil players. If Noah is Good, then the two Evil players must come from the remaining three of us (Leo, Amara, and myself)—which mathematically guarantees that at least one of Leo or Amara is Evil. So ask yourself: do you genuinely believe Noah and I are the Evil pair? Noah has been speaking with complete earnestness, while he and I are on completely opposite sides of this debate. If you believe Noah has any chance of being Good, then taking both Leo and Amara guarantees placing at least one Evil player on Mission 2. Swapping in Noah isn't just taking a random gamble on an untested player; it avoids putting both seats into a pair where, unless Noah and I are both Evil, at least one of them is compromised. Elena, as leader with the power to revise this proposal before the vote, do you truly believe Noah and I are both Evil, or will you break up the Leo-Amara pair and include Noah?

Arjun, you are right that this team is entirely Good only if you and Noah are both Evil. But the same arithmetic applies to any team I propose: swapping Amara for Noah would require you and Amara to be the Evil pair for the new team to be entirely Good. Noah and you disagreeing does not rule out your being teammates, nor does it prove it.

Mission 1's success gives Leo and Amara some evidence in their favor, but how much depends on whether an Evil player would conceal themselves. I don't know anyone else's alignment and won't claim certainty. For now, I prefer to retain the successful pair rather than swap in Noah without a stronger reason.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
